The basis of this view is the denial that universals exist at all, since both genus and differentia are universals.
Thinkers of this tendency hold that universals are nothing more than conventional names and that a definition does nothing more than explain the meaning of a word.
On this basis, we might say that there is some relationship between this tendency and the doctrine of “nominalism” known in medieval Europe.
But the similarity is only formal. This Arab tendency did not contain the materialist position that was present in nominalism.
(b) The Law of the Excluded Middle
This question is also known as “the principle of the excluded third.”

Although this principle is one of the basic principles on which Aristotelian logical demonstration rests, there was a major logician in medieval Arab-Islamic thought who disagreed: Abū Sulaymān al-Manṭiqī al-Sijistānī (d. 990 CE). We have already quoted a clear passage in which he argues that it is not impossible for both sides of a contradiction to be false. In fact, his wording suggests that he regarded this as quite straightforward. But he still believed that two contradictory statements could never both be true at the same time.

The law of causality is one of the basic principles of demonstrative reasoning in Aristotelian logic. In Aristotle’s system, the validity of a proof depends on the assumption that there is a self-evident connection between cause and effect.

The Ashʿarites, along with some Muʿtazilite theologians, rejected this law at its foundation. Arab-Islamic philosophers, by contrast, relied on causality throughout their logical and philosophical work.

Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī was one of its leading critics. He wrote extensively against the principle of causality and argued that what people call cause and effect is really a matter of habit. People repeatedly see two things or two events occurring together, he says, until they come to “imagine that the connection between them exists because one is the cause of the other.”
This view is similar to positions later taken by modern philosophers such as Malebranche, Berkeley, and Hume.

In Chapter Seven, we examined the relationship between language and thought. We argued that even the Arabic name for the science of logic, manṭiq, gives evidence that Arab thinkers understood this relationship as both ontological and dialectical. We also quoted passages from their writings on logic that show how deeply they understood it.

Because of this, they added new discussions of how words convey meaning. These additions enriched the part of logic concerned with concepts. And although these discussions may look linguistic on the surface, Arab logicians succeeded in giving them a genuinely logical character.
We also examined the categories in relation to both logic and philosophy.

The categories are abstract concepts, and they helped philosophy develop and use the language of abstraction. This language is essential to philosophy because philosophy represents the highest form of abstraction.

We saw that Aristotle treated the categories as general and universal attributes of existing things—in other words, as their kinds and genera. We then showed that this basis reveals the material content of the categories.
Arab logicians and philosophers approached them on the same basis. We pointed in particular to the positions of Ibn Sīnā, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Rushd.

Our study showed that the Aristotelian approach remained the dominant one in Arab discussions of the categories. Only a small number of thinkers removed the categories from logic and placed them instead within metaphysics.
At the end of the chapter, we examined Aristotle’s different forms of reasoning and the different ways knowledge can be reached: syllogistic proof, induction, definition, and analogy.

We found that Arab logicians greatly expanded the study of propositions and the forms of the syllogism. Alongside categorical propositions, they developed the study of conditional propositions, which Aristotle’s logic had not examined. They also added the fourth figure of the syllogism, which Aristotle had left out of his own logical system.
When it came to induction, however, we found that Arab logicians added nothing substantial to what Aristotle had already discussed.

They explained this limitation by pointing to the level reached by the natural sciences in both the Greek and medieval periods. Scientific tools and methods had not yet developed far enough to let logicians and philosophers examine a sufficiently large number of individual cases and then move from them to general laws with certainty rather than probability.
That is one side of the matter.

There was another problem as well. Logic had been restricted largely to the service of Islamic and Christian theology. This prevented the law of causality from being fully used in induction—or in inductive proof—to discover general laws of nature and society with certainty.
We also found an important difference between Aristotle’s use of analogy and the Arab understanding of reasoning by analogy.
For Aristotle, analogy meant reaching a judgment by relying on a direct similarity between one particular case and another.

Arab thinkers, however, based the similarity between two particular cases on the idea of causality. They tried to discover a cause for the judgment that was shared by two things with similar qualities and circumstances.
There was, of course, a fundamental difference between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites in what they meant by “cause.”
